name: LV mass index
seoTitle: LV mass index Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: LV mass index: work out pWd from the weight and the iVSd. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The LV mass index calculator turns the weight, the iVSd and more into pWd. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the LV mass index calculator work?
sections.html:
The LV mass index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pWd in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the weight, the iVSd, the left ventricular mass and the LVMI.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the LV mass index calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

PWd=-iVSd − LVEDD − 1 ÷ 52 × (26 ^ 2 ÷ 3) × (-104 × (LVEDD ^ 3) − 125 × left ventricular mass + the square root of (10816 × (LVEDD ^ 6) + 26000 × (LVEDD ^ 3) × left ventricular mass − 15600 × (LVEDD ^ 3) + 15625 × (left ventricular mass ^ 2) − 18750 × left ventricular mass + 5625) + 75)
Body surface area=left ventricular mass ÷ LVMI
PWd=(1 ÷ 2) × LVEDD × relative wall thickness (RWT)
Height=3600 × (body surface area ^ 2) ÷ weight

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Sex set to Female, Do you know body surface area? set to Yes, LVEDD = 30 mm and IVSd = 30 mm. The calculator returns PWd = -60 mm and Relative wall thickness (RWT) = -4.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: PWd = -60 mm and Relative wall thickness (RWT) = -4 should be roughly the size you expected from Sex set to Female and Do you know body surface area? set to Yes.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Mass, opening in grams

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The LV mass index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the weight, the iVSd and the left ventricular mass — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the LV mass index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pWd, derived from the weight, the iVSd and the left ventricular mass. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the LV mass index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the weight, the iVSd, the left ventricular mass and the LVMI, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports PWd = -60 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the LV mass index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
